To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
β2-gly-coprotein I concentration is controlled by a single autosomal co-diminant locus with two alleles, BgD and BgA, which are responsible for the two phenotypes, BgD (deficient) and BgA (normal).

β2-glyco-protein I serum concentration is controlled by a pair (or pairs) of autosomal co-dominator genes, and that the gene(s) responsible for β2-glyceroprotein I deficiency is (are) different from the gene(s) which control(s) its serum concentration.

the concentration of β2-GPI in serum is genetically controlled, that the inheritance of β2-GP1 concentration is co-dominant and autosomal, that the inheritance is not linked to the HLA complex, and that there are at least two different genes, one for the normal and the other one for the low β2-GPI concentration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic control of a serum protein, the concentration of which is subject to considerable individual variation.
the genetic control of a plasma protein.
the identification of the gene(s) controlling β2-glyco-protein I concentration and with the study of the genetic control of this protein.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the concentration of β2 glycoprotein I in human serum is controlled by a pair autosomal alleles which are expressed in a co-dominant manner.
β2-glyco-protein I concentration is controlled by a pair or alleles which are transmitted in autosomal co-domination.
the β2-glyco-protein I deficiency gene BgDI, which is transmitted as an autosomal dominant, is the cause of the low serum concentrations in the families with the type I pattern of inheritance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
β2-glyco-protein I is a protein with two genetic variants, BgF and BgD, which have different serum concentrations.
the concentration of β2-GPI in human serum is controlled by two autosomal alleles BgA and BgD.
β2-gly coprotein I concentration in serum is controlled by at least 3 alleles: A, a and BgD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are at least two genetic types with different levels of β2-glycerophosphatase.
the genetic control of the concentration of β2 glycoprotein I in serum is complex.
